newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel reopens tunnel, talks tough.
newsitem.headline: Israel reopens tunnel, talks tough.

text.p: Israel reopened a controversial tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem on Sunday while U.S. and U.N. mediators tried to bridge "wide gaps" over an Israeli-PLO summit to end violence.

The Clinton administration, fearing its Middle East peace policy could unravel five weeks before the U.S. presidential election, sought to bring Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu together in Washington as soon as Wednesday, diplomatic sources said.

But they said the two sides were far apart with Arafat insisting the tunnel be closed and Netanyahu vowing to keep it open. Fifty-five Palestinians and 14 Israeli soldiers have died in clashes over the tunnel.

Israeli officials raised the spectre of disarming Palestinian police if gunbattles resumed. More Israeli tanks moved into positions around PLO-ruled areas of the West Bank and Gaza, witnesses said. Palestinian police said they were closely watching the Israeli moves which they interpreted as sabre-rattling.

Security sources said Israel had implemented the first phase of "Operation Field of Thorns", a plan whose final third stage is the retaking of West Bank and Gaza areas handed over to Arafat under the 1993 Oslo self-rule agreement.
The sources said the army had no intention at present of implementing the final phase which would amount to a war with Arafat's more than 30,000 lightly armed police.
Foreign military analysts and diplomats believe Arafat would leave Gaza if Netanyahu's right-wing government scrapped the self-rule Oslo accord.

Palestinian stone-throwers clashed with Israeli soldiers in sporadic unrest but the West Bank and Gaza were quieter than they had been since Netanyahu opened the archaeological tunnel which Palestinians see as an illegal act on occupied land and an assault on Moslem holy places.
Youths hurled stones when the tunnel's new second entrance from the Old City's Moslem Quarter was opened after the Jewish sabbath. The protests were quickly quelled by police.

Many foreign governments and the Israeli opposition have called Netanyahu's move a blunder which Arafat has exploited to shore up his standing among Palestinians, deeply frustrated with Oslo and Israeli foot-dragging over self-rule implementation.

The United States, however, has tried to shield its strongest regional ally. It cast the lone abstention when the 14 other members of the U.N. Security Council called for the safety and protection of Palestinian civilians to be ensured and for the immediate resumption of the Middle East peace process on Saturday.

"Talks are going on but the gaps are wide," mediator Terje Larsen said. "But I believe the gaps can be bridged because it is in the deep interest of both sides," Larsen, who is the United Nations coordinator in Palestinian areas, told Reuters.

"If there is no solution on the political and security level the alternative is a bloodbath on a massive scale with regional repercussions and catastrophic political implications. Both sides are very aware of this," Larsen added.
As the diplomacy continued, both sides stepped up the rhetoric.
Netanyahu aide David Bar-Illan said Israel should consider disarming Palestinian police if fighting resumes.

"For now we aren't thinking of that. But if such things will continue and such incidents will recur, we will have to think about that also," Bar-Illan told Israel Radio. He ruled out a summit before violence stopped.

Bar-Illan said Israel would also have to rethink its long-delayed handover of parts of the West Bank City of Hebron to Palestinian rule in light of the gunfights that erupted between its soldiers and Palestinian police.

Diplomatic sources said Arafat insisted on immediate Hebron redeployment, a timetable for futher Oslo implementation, and the closure of the tunnel ahead of a meeting with Netanyahu. He rejected a proposal to meet Netanyahy one-on-one before the wider Washington summit.
Arafat wants Egyptian and other participation at the meeting as a counterweight to Israel's closeness to the United States, the sources said.

"The venue and substance of the meeting between President Arafat and Netanyahu are being discussed. We want resumption of final-status talks and automatic implementation of accords. They must close the tunnel," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters.

Marwan Kanafani, a Palestinian legislator, said: "President Arafat until dawn has had intensive contacts over the American invitation and he welcomed it, but it seems the Israelis are foot-dragging on the invitation and are exploiting the American sensitive position ahead of elections."
"We are prepared to discuss any serious proposal that will lead to ending Palestinian bloodshed, an end to Israeli threats of reoccupation and restore our rights," he told Reuters.
